subject: Cypher Labs dedicated capacity sizing — token stress test & headroom

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>

Subject: Cypher Labs dedicated capacity sizing — token stress test & headroom

Hi Alan / Sofia,

Following our call this morning, attached is a first-pass sizing workbook that maps your expected token profile to dedicated GPU slabs and headroom. The sheet includes a baseline tokens/sec estimate tied to your sample traffic (concurrency 120, avg request 350 tokens) and a few model options (redwood/gpt-medium-q8, community/llama2-13b,/redwood/opt-13b-4bit).

Key assumptions in the model:
- Peak concurrency: 120 simultaneous sessions (bursty window ~3m)
- Avg tokens per request: 350
- p95 latency SLO target: 250ms for generation-only paths
- Headroom target: 1.8x steady-state; 2.2x for peak burst windows in the contract tier

We call out where caching or prefix warmup reduces required slab counts and where quantized variants materially change per-token GPU throughput. If you prefer, Ben can run a quick simulation with your actual request traces next week.

Attachments: cypher_capacity_model_v1.xlsx, cypher_p95_latency_profile.pdf

Next steps I propose:
1) You confirm whether the 120 concurrency and 350 token average reflect expected Q3 traffic (or send us a 48-hour trace).
2) Ben & Priyom validate the model against your tail-latency requirements and propose a burst policy (reserved vs. on-demand).
3) We draft a committed slab recommendation and an option for on-call burst credits for the first 90 days.

Thanks — happy to jump on a follow-up with engineers if helpful.

-Kim

Subject: Re: Cypher Labs dedicated capacity sizing — token stress test & headroom

Kim — thanks for the fast turnaround and the workbook. A few quick clarifications from our side:

1) Concurrency: the 120 is a conservative estimate; typical daytime peak is ~90 but we do see short spikes to 180 during product launches. Those spikes last 1-4 minutes.
2) Token mix: 70% of requests are short (<= 150 tokens), 25% mid (150-600), 5% long (>600). The 350 average in your sheet aligns with sample but skews high for our normal workload.
3) Latency: the 250ms p95 is aggressive — our internal UI tolerates up to 400ms for some flows, but the chat experience target is 250ms. We want to hotspot the critical path (chat) on the lower-latency slab.

Question: your sheet shows a headroom multiplier of 1.8x -> how sensitive is the slab recommendation to that number? If we accept 1.5x for steady-state and a 2.5x burst buffer via pre-warmed on-demand, what changes?

Also can you confirm whether the quantized variant reduces GPUs by 20-35% in your benchmarking for our workload?

Appreciate it — happy to have Ben do the trace run.

—Alan
Alan Nguyen
CTO, Cypher Labs
alan.nguyen@cypherlabs.ai
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Cypher Labs dedicated capacity sizing — token stress test & headroom

Quick internal note before I reply to Alan directly:

- If Alan's normal peak is 90 and spikes to 180 for <5 minutes, we can keep committed slabs sized to sustain 1.5x steady-state (saves cost) and configure a short burst pool with pre-warmed slots that auto-attach for 1-5 minute windows. That lets us guarantee chat p95 without overcommitting.
- Quantization: for the redwood/gpt-medium-q8 path we see ~28-33% GPU slot savings vs fp16 on their token mix (because typical sequences are short and KV cache fits well). For larger community models (llama2-13b) benefits are lower (~18-22%) depending on attention packing.
- Slab math: using Alan's traffic distribution, the workbook's current model overestimates required steady slabs by about 15% (because the average of 350 tokens assumes heavier long-request tail). I'll update the model with the distribution split.

I'll respond to Alan with a revised recommendation and simulated p95 curves by end of day. Priyom, can you add an ops-level note on fallback policy (route to hosted smaller model / throttling) and the estimated cost delta?

Ben
Ben Carter
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com
From: Priyom Das <priyom.das@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Cypher Labs dedicated capacity sizing — token stress test & headroom

Alan / Sofia — following Ben's note, we've updated the spreadsheet to include two proposal lanes:

Lane A — Cost-optimized committed slabs
- Steady-state headroom: 1.5x
- Committed GPUs: 8 x A100-equivalent (quantized stack assumed for core chat model)
- Burst: 6 pre-warmed on-demand slots (attach for 1-5 minute spikes)
- Expected p95 (chat path): ~230ms under steady peak, ~360ms during extreme spikes (with burst attach it drops to ~240ms)
- Notes: ~22% lower monthly cost vs 1.8x committed approach; 90-day ramp recommended.

Lane B — SLA-focused dedicated slabs
- Steady-state headroom: 1.8x
- Committed GPUs: 11 x A100-equivalent (mix of q8 and fp16 for fallback)
- Burst: 4 pre-warmed slots for microbursts, auto-fallback to hosted variants if sustained beyond 6 minutes
- Expected p95 (chat path): ~210ms steady, ~230ms with short spikes
- Notes: higher committed cost but simpler operational envelope and stronger latency guarantees.

Attachments updated: cypher_capacity_model_v1.xlsx (rev 2) — includes per-slot tokens/sec, quantization delta, and a p95 simulation tab.

If you prefer, we can convert Lane A into a phased commit: start 60% Lane A for months 1-3, then move to Lane B if Q4 traffic materializes. I can export the per-hour simulated trace if you want to run it against your feature-flagged UI.

Next steps suggestion:
- Alan: pick Lane A (phased) vs Lane B (SLA), or ask for a hybrid phasing schedule.
- If Lane A phased: sign commitment addendum for the initial slab and we schedule an ops runbook for the pre-warm attach logic.

Thanks — happy to hop on a 30m technical walkthrough this week.

-Priyom
Priyom Das
